title: When Food Aid Shrinks, a San Diego Office Doubles as a Food Pantry
summary:
It should have been her day off. Instead, early one Saturday morning, Rosa Rodarte was back at her social services office in San Diego, pushing carts of groceries and loading them into people's cars.

Rodarte's usual job is helping people apply for programs like food assistance. Lately, she has been handing out the food itself. 'We have the same goal,' she says. 'We want to make sure everybody is being helped and not judged.'

The program at the center of the story is SNAP, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which helps people with low incomes buy groceries. Over the past year, about five million people across the country have lost those benefits. The drop followed a sweeping tax and spending law, the One Big Beautiful Bill, signed in July 2025. It cut SNAP funding, tightened who can qualify, and ended food aid for most asylum seekers and refugees. It is the fastest decline in decades.

In San Diego County, 36,000 fewer people were on SNAP this September than in July 2025. The county teamed up with local food banks to hand out free groceries at its offices. Between August and September, the events gave out nearly 70,000 pounds of food to more than 5,200 people. County leaders say it is not a long-term fix, but they did not want to stand by while neighbors went hungry.

The changes have also added work for the people who run the program. New work requirements apply to groups including homeless people, former foster youth, veterans, and parents with a child older than 14. Supporters of the changes, including U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, argue they bring back the dignity of work. Workers say many people on SNAP already work, and the rules mean more paperwork.
why_it_matters: When millions of people lose help buying food, the effects show up in ordinary neighborhoods, where offices and food banks have to fill the gap. The debate over work requirements shapes who gets help and how hard it is to keep it.

background_read: SNAP is a government program that helps people with low incomes buy groceries, usually by giving them money on a card to spend at food stores.
People have to meet certain rules to qualify, and those rules can change when lawmakers pass new tax and spending laws.
When people lose that help, food banks step in: they collect donated food and hand it out for free to families in need.
County social services offices normally help people sign up for aid, but some have started handing out groceries directly while neighbors go hungry.
